DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Introducing an Off-Peak Membership
Pulse Fitness, Commercial Team, August 2026

1. Proposal
We propose introducing an off-peak membership at £29 a month from 1 October 2026, alongside our existing standard membership at £42 a month. Off-peak members would have access before 4 pm on weekdays and all day at weekends, with full access to the gym floor and to classes running in those hours.

2. Background
Pulse operates four clubs with 9,600 standard members. Membership has been flat for 18 months, while two budget gyms have opened within our catchments, both offering memberships at £22 to £25 a month. Our clubs are busy between 5 pm and 8 pm on weekdays, when the gym floor often runs at or near capacity, but quiet during weekday daytimes, when typical utilisation is around 30%.

Access-control data for May to July 2026 show that 31% of our current standard members visit exclusively in what would be the off-peak window, and a further 22% visit mostly off-peak.

3. Market evidence
A survey of 640 non-members living within two miles of our clubs, conducted in June, found that 19% would "definitely" or "probably" join at £29 a month for off-peak access. The most interested groups were retirees, shift workers, parents of school-age children and students.

Four of our six closest competitors already offer an off-peak or daytime membership, priced between £25 and £32.

4. Classes and retention
Retention is the other half of our commercial challenge. Monthly churn among members who attend at least one class a week is 2.1%, against 4.8% among members who do not attend classes. Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week to support the new membership, which should lower churn among off-peak members towards the 2.1% level. The additional classes would cost £18,700 a month across the four clubs in instructor fees.

5. Revenue projection
We expect to recruit 1,200 new off-peak members in the first year, about 300 per club, which is consistent with the survey response and the size of our catchments. At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue. After the cost of the additional classes (£224,400 a year), net additional revenue is £193,200 a year.

Because daytime utilisation is low, the additional members can be accommodated without investment in equipment or space.

6. Operational changes
Access control will be updated so that off-peak members' cards do not open the turnstiles outside their access window. Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm, giving those finishing early shifts or school pick-ups time to train. Members will be able to upgrade to standard membership at any time, and to switch between membership types with one month's notice.

7. Risks
Some standard members may perceive the off-peak price as unfair. We will communicate the change as an extension of choice. Competitor responses are possible; the budget gyms already price below our proposed off-peak rate, so we do not expect a price war.

8. Staff consultation
Club managers and front-of-house teams at all four clubs were consulted in July. Managers supported the proposal, noting that daytime classes are often under-filled and that a daytime membership would help build a regular community at quieter times. Front-of-house staff asked for clear signage and app messaging about access hours, which we will provide before launch.

9. Recommendation
The off-peak membership fills spare daytime capacity, responds to competitor offers and targets clearly identified customer groups. We project net additional revenue of around £193,000 a year and recommend launch on 1 October 2026.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm" -- Section 1 defines off-peak access as before 4 pm on weekdays; section 6 says off-peak members have weekday access until 5 pm (also into the busy 5-8 pm period the document says is near capacity). The access window contradicts itself.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week" -- The churn difference is correlational: members who choose to attend classes weekly are likely more engaged/committed to begin with (self-selection). It does not show classes cause lower churn, nor that adding classes would bring off-peak churn to 2.1%.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue." -- The projection counts only new members and ignores downgrades, although the document states 31% of the 9,600 standard members (about 2,976) already visit only off-peak and can switch with one month's notice. If they downgraded, revenue would fall by about £13 x 2,976 = £38,700 a month (about £464,000 a year), more than wiping out the projected gain.

REVIEW:
# Review: Off-Peak Membership Proposal

The proposal's central revenue figure of £193,200 a year is not reliable. The largest problem is a cost the document never counts. Several of the supporting claims are also weaker than the author's summary suggests.

## 1. Cannibalisation is ignored

This is the decisive flaw. Section 2 says 31% of current standard members (about 2,976 people) already visit only in the off-peak window, and another 22% visit mostly off-peak. Section 6 lets members switch between membership types on one month's notice. Each exclusive off-peak member who moves from £42 to £29 costs £13 a month, or £156 a year.

- If all 2,976 exclusive off-peak members switched, the loss would be about £464,000 a year, more than twice the projected net gain.
- The proposal breaks even if only about 1,240 members downgrade. That is roughly 13% of all standard members, or about 42% of the exclusive off-peak group.
- If the "mostly off-peak" group were also tempted, the exposure would be larger still.

The only direction the document mentions is upgrading ("Members who want more can upgrade at any time"). The real risk is the opposite direction. Section 7 reduces this risk to a perception-of-fairness issue, which understates it. The projection also ignores prospects who would have joined at £42 but now choose £29.

## 2. The "spare capacity" evidence is narrower than the claim

- The 30% utilisation figure covers weekday daytimes only. The offer includes all day at weekends, and no weekend utilisation data is given.
- The window is inconsistent. Section 1 says weekday access before 4 pm, and Section 6 says until 5 pm. The 4–5 pm hour is the shoulder of the 5–8 pm peak, and the document doesn't show whether it is quiet.
- "Costs us almost nothing" sits awkwardly beside £224,400 a year in new class costs.

## 3. The retention argument confuses correlation with causation

Members who attend classes churn less (2.1% against 4.8%), but engaged members are the ones who choose to attend classes. This does not show that adding classes will cut off-peak churn "towards the 2.1% level". The £224,400 class spend rests on that assumption.

Section 8 also undercuts the need for the extra classes. Managers say daytime classes are "often under-filled", so existing capacity could serve new members at no extra cost.

## 4. The projection treats 1,200 members as in place for all twelve months

- It assumes no ramp-up, so all 1,200 members pay from 1 October.
- It assumes no churn. Even at the document's own 2.1% monthly rate, about 22% of a cohort leaves within a year. At 4.8%, about 44% does.
- Realistic first-year revenue is therefore well below £417,600, while the class cost is fixed.
- Other costs are omitted: marketing, signage and app work, access-control changes, extra staffing and cleaning.

## 5. The demand evidence is weak

- The survey found that 19% of 640 respondents (about 120 people) would "definitely or probably" join. Stated intent routinely overstates actual sign-ups, and the "probably" responses are the least reliable.
- No catchment population or conversion assumption links this to 1,200 members. "Consistent with the survey" and "conservative" are asserted, not shown.
- The survey doesn't say how respondents were recruited, and it tested only £29, so it says nothing about price sensitivity.
- The target groups are plausible but not sized. Shift workers and students may not fit a weekday-daytime window.

## 6. The competitor evidence is thin

- Four of six competitors offering off-peak plans at £25–£32 shows £29 is within the range. It does not show demand.
- The budget gyms, which are the actual cause of flat membership, charge £22–£25 for what is presumably full-hours access. Off-peak at £29 doesn't beat them. "We do not expect a price war" is an assertion without support.

## 7. The "independent sources" framing is misleading

The access data, survey and competitor pricing all support a gross-demand story. None addresses what happens to existing revenue. Describing the case as multiple independent sources of evidence overstates its strength when the same gap undermines all of them.

## Recommendations

1. Model cannibalisation explicitly with scenarios of 5%, 15% and 30% of exclusive off-peak members downgrading, and show net revenue under each.
2. Consider design changes to limit downgrades, such as a switching lock-in period, a narrower window, or a higher price.
3. Fix the 4 pm / 5 pm inconsistency and provide weekend utilisation data.
4. Rebuild the projection with a monthly ramp, churn, and the full cost base.
5. Fill existing under-filled daytime classes first, and treat added classes as a pilot, not a committed cost.
6. Document the survey method and tie conversion assumptions to the catchment population.

As written, the recommendation to launch is not supported. The net figure could easily be zero or negative.
